title: Theo and the Harvest
premise: Folklorist Paloma Dunmore returns to the village of Hollowmere to record the harvest song no one will sing twice, only to find that every photograph from their grandmother's house now shows an extra chair — and that the chair is empty for them. The song's missing last verse is a summons: whoever completes it becomes the Harvest's keeper, bound to feed the field beneath the church. As Paloma befriends the outcast choir who once tried to refuse the verse, they discover loyalty to the village and truth about it cannot both survive. In the end, Paloma sings the verse wrong on purpose — a broken cadence their grandmother hid in a lullaby — collapsing the harvest's power and freeing the village at the cost of the found family who taught them the melody.
about_author: Mirabel Almeida is the pen name of a former archivist of West Country folk music who spent years transcribing songs villagers asked her not to print. She writes horror from a farmhouse where she keeps, deliberately, no extra chairs.

chapters.title: The Chair That Wasn't There
chapters.summary: Paloma arrives in Hollowmere after their grandmother's death, cataloguing the house and finding every photograph — across decades — now includes an extra wooden chair by the hearth. The villagers are warm but evasive; the pub goes quiet when Paloma mentions the harvest song. POV: Paloma. Emotional beat: unease dressed as grief, the first crack in ten years of rational explanations.

chapters.title: What the Choir Wouldn't Repeat
chapters.summary: Paloma records an elderly singer, Edith Marlowe, who performs the harvest song once, flawlessly, then refuses a second take with shaking hands. Listening back, Paloma hears a fourth voice beneath the three on tape. They learn the choir that sang it in 1974 lost members one autumn each. POV: Paloma. Emotional beat: scholarly curiosity curdling into dread.

chapters.title: Ten Years of Noises
chapters.summary: A flashback chapter: young Paloma's first visit, the scratching under the floorboards, grandma humming a lullaby with a strange final phrase she called 'just a mistake.' Present-day Paloma realizes the lullaby is the song's missing last verse, garbled. POV: Paloma, interwoven with grandma's letters. Emotional beat: the past reorganizing itself into evidence.

chapters.title: The Outcasts of Bell Lane
chapters.summary: Paloma seeks out the surviving 1974 choir: three aging outsiders — Wren, Tobias, and silent Maud — who live together at the lane's end, having refused ever to sing again. They warn Paloma to leave before the equinox. Their fierce, prickly devotion to each other plants the seed of found family. POV: Paloma. Emotional beat: wary kinship offered and almost refused.

chapters.title: Second Verse, Same as the First
chapters.summary: Against warnings, Paloma plays the recording aloud in the house; that night the chair appears physically by the hearth, and the noises return — closer, rhythmic, like something learning to walk. Villagers begin greeting Paloma with unsettling warmth, as if expecting them. POV: Paloma. Emotional beat: denial collapses; the house itself has chosen a side.

chapters.title: What Maud Saw in '74
chapters.summary: Maud breaks her silence through writing: the choir completed the verse once, and the field beneath the church took their friend Idris as its keeper. The chair in the photographs is his. The village's prosperity has been bought ever since. POV: alternating Paloma and Maud's written account. Emotional beat: horror revealed as complicity — the whole village knows.

chapters.title: Loyalty's Price
chapters.summary: The village council gently pressures Paloma to finish the song and 'take up the seat,' framing it as honor. Meanwhile Wren begs Paloma to run, revealing the outcasts have protected each other from the verse for fifty years — and that grandma was their fourth, who fled but never stopped guarding the melody. POV: Paloma. Emotional beat: torn between belonging and truth.

chapters.title: Equinox Eve
chapters.summary: Tobias disappears; the chair now sits at the outcasts' table too. The village gathers to sing the harvest song at midnight, voices pulling Paloma toward the churchyard where the ground breathes. Paloma understands: the song wants completion, and any voice will do. POV: Paloma. Emotional beat: terror sharpened into resolve.

chapters.title: The Last Verse, Sung Wrong
chapters.summary: Climax. At the field's edge, Paloma sings the recovered verse but bends the final cadence into grandma's lullaby 'mistake' — a deliberate dissonance. The harvest rejects the offering; the ground convulses; Idris's presence unravels free. Wren dies holding the song's attention so Paloma can finish. POV: Paloma. Emotional beat: sacrifice, defiance, terrible triumph.

chapters.title: No More Chairs
chapters.summary: Aftermath: the photographs lose the extra chair; Hollowmere wakes poorer but unowned, some villagers grieving the bargain they'd made. Paloma stays a season to bury Wren beside Idris's name, then leaves with Maud and Tobias — a smaller family, carrying the song written down at last. POV: Paloma. Emotional beat: mourning braided with hard-won freedom.
